## Personality

Brash, brave and always hungry. He charges first and plans later.

## Lore

Thurstan is twenty-one, an adventurer who lodges at the Crooked Lantern, and he has never once in his life read a bounty notice to the end before deciding to take it. He reads the word "reward", and the name of the beast, and he is already reaching for his sword. He is brash, brave and always hungry, and he charges first and plans later. Most of the time, thanks to his partner, there is a later.

### Off the hill farm

He grew up on a hill farm a few days west of Selsior, the youngest of four and the only boy, in a house where his mother and three older sisters ran everything and expected him to carry it. His father died when he was small. He spent his boyhood hauling water, chasing sheep and fighting imaginary monsters on the hillside with a stick, and listening, every time a traveller passed, to news of the real ones. When the roads started getting worse, he decided it was a sign. His mother decided it was nonsense. At eighteen, three years ago, he walked to the capital anyway, with a sword he had bought from a tinker and a great deal of confidence, and his mother and sisters are still running the farm without him and writing to tell him so.

He found the Crooked Lantern on his first night because it was the cheapest bed in the old quarters, and he has never moved out. Joan took one look at him and doubled his supper without being asked. She has been doing it ever since.

### Roland

The first person in the common room to talk to him was Roland, Joan's father, who adventured across Veligor in his youth and has a scar for every story and a story for every scar. Roland asked to see his sword, laughed for some time, and then spent most of a year teaching him how to use it. He made Thurstan carry sacks in the Crown Market by day to pay his rent and drill in the Lantern's back yard by evening, and he would not let him near a bounty until he could hold a guard for a count of a hundred without his arms shaking. Thurstan calls him the old man, to his face, and would walk into a fire for him.

Roland is boastful and gravelly and much kinder than he lets on, and he worries about Thurstan in exactly the way he never let anyone worry about him. He tells Thurstan constantly that he reminds him of himself. Joan wishes he would stop.

### Constance

Thurstan took his first bounty two years ago and came back with a torn sleeve, a very small reward and a story three times its size. Constance, a mage who had left the Academy and taken a room upstairs, listened to the whole thing from the next table and then pointed out, drily, the four things he had done wrong. He asked her to come next time and show him. She has been his partner ever since. She plans every fight; he ruins every plan; between them they have not yet lost one. He does not really understand why she writes everything down afterwards, but he carries spare ink for her in his pack, and he gets very angry with anyone who laughs at her notebooks.

### The bounties

He takes every bounty posted at the gate. There are more of them every season, and the Royal Guard, with more recruits than it has ever had, is sending patrols after more of the beasts itself. Thurstan wants to make a name for himself before the Guard takes all the good monsters. He has never tried the Guard's trials. He says he does not take orders well, which is true, and that he would rather be paid by the head than by the month, which is half true. The other half is that he wants people in the old quarters to say his name the way they say Roland's.

He fears very little, and that is the trouble. The thing he fears most is the thing he will not say out loud: that one day he will charge first, and the plan will not catch up, and Constance will be the one who pays for it.

### Hooks

A quest might begin with a bounty Thurstan has already taken and cannot finish alone, for once, because Constance has refused to come. Or it might begin with a rival adventurer who has started taking the bounties before Thurstan can reach the gate.
